items.title: Under the influence: how creator marketing upended advertising
items.author: Mark Sweney
items.content:
Brands are piggybacking off the potential sales that targeting millions of ardent followers can bring – but there are risks

From the Avon ladies to the former Sex Pistols lead singer John Lydon selling butter, personal endorsement of products is a well-trodden form of marketing with significant gains – and pitfalls. More recently, the practice of teaming up with social media influencers has become a boom in the ad industry over the last decade – and came firmly into the spotlight this week.

First, the Guardian revealed that Unilever, the consumer goods behemoth behind huge brands including Dove soap to Hellmann’s mayonnaise, had slashed its almost £100m TV ad budget and was ploughing funds into online influencer marketing instead.

items.title: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
items.author: Claire Jackson
items.content:
A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebook

It often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!

Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

Claire Jackson is a journalist who writes about classical music, art and animals

items.title: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings
items.author: Helena Horton
items.content:
Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue

Restaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.

This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.

items.title: Village plea for replacement Royal Mail postbox hits the rocks (literally)
items.author: Anna Tims
items.content:
Residents woke up to find their vital box missing, but despite 11 months of lobbying the company now says it cannot replace it

Residents of a remote Devon village now have to drive more than a mile to send letters after their attempts to get a new postbox literally hit the rocks.

Villagers in North Huish have described a farcical near 11-month battle to challenge Royal Mail’s excuses after their box vanished without warning last January.

items.title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst
items.author: Alexander Hurst
items.content:
Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking

Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.

On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there. Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris

items.author: Sandra Haurant
items.content:
From small fixes such as decluttering to taking your property off the market for a break, there are ways to seal the deal

Selling your home is always a big task, but when the headlines are telling you prices are falling, it can feel even more daunting.

items.title: Stunted sprouts: heatwaves and drought take toll on festive vegetable
items.author: Joanna Partridge
items.content:
The Christmas staple is smaller this year after a hot, dry summer hit the water-loving – but versatile – brassica

They are a key ingredient in many Christmas dinners, but brussels sprouts appearing on diners’ plates this festive season are likely to be smaller than usual, after the hot, dry summer took its toll on the water-loving crop.

Sprouts are generally planted outdoors between March and early June, meaning they were already in the ground when the UK faced a series of heatwaves and drought conditions across Wales and most of England.

items.title: Could AI break encryption? What mathematical breakthroughs mean for cybersecurity
items.author: Aisha Down
items.content:
Experts suggest AI companies may be sitting on ‘bombshell’ that could have severe consequences for secret information

Leading experts and the governor of the Bank of England have suggested that top AI companies might have something under their hat – a “bombshell” revelation about encryption. Depending on what it is, it could have major consequences for the world’s secret information, and the banks and governments that hold and transmit it.

This is because of recent, startling mathematical advances made by AI models, which are still being understood.

items.title: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts warn
items.author: Aisha Down
items.content:
Exclusive: AI may have cracked decades-old maths problems that underpin encryption at banks and government agencies

AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.

Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.

items.title: The explosion of extreme wealth is the major problem of our time | Bernie Sanders
items.author: Bernie Sanders
items.content:
At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class

We are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class.

Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.”

Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.content:
Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.

items.content:

Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter.

items.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights
items.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
items.content:
Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances

Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

items.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
items.content:
Department stores are hosting in-person events for those who find comfort in collecting the British soft toy brand

They’re cute, cuddly and taking over the homes of young adults.

Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult buyers as they snap up signature smiley designs in the shape of everything from croissants and disco balls to turtles and teabags.

items.title: ‘Punched in the guts’: Poundland staff left reeling as it goes into administration
items.author: Sarah Butler and Josh Halliday
items.content:
Workers are sad but unsurprised as closures and job losses loom, while 2,000 suppliers will take a big hit

“I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it.

While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty.

items.author: Mark Sweney
items.content:
Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

Brands know use of agents such as Meta Muse is on the rise but are unlikely to hand them the keys to the shop

They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.

This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money.

items.author: Presented by Michael Safi with Dan Milmo ; producer Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
items.content:
The Trump administration has approved Elon Musk’s plan to create datacentres in space. US federal regulators have authorised the launch of one million Starmind orbital satellites, which are built by Musk’s SpaceX, to process data in space. Supporters argue the project will be more energy-efficient and reduce the environmental impact of datacentres on Earth as the AI industry grows. items.title: Some old-school advice for Burnham: boost competition if you want growth | Nils Pratley
items.author: Nils Pratley
items.content:
Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’

The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government.

Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”.

items.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee
items.author: Polly Toynbee
items.content:
High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1

When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.author: Anonymous
items.content:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.title: Huge flames rise from fire at Bangkok oil facility – video
items.content:
Thailand's Bangchak Corporation said on Thursday it had shut down all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery after a fire. Video showed flames and thick black smoke rising above the facility after the fire broke out at about 2.45pm local time. The blaze was brought under control and extinguished about 30 minutes later, the company said in a statement.

The cause of the fire at the refinery, which has a maximum capacity of 120,000 barrels per day, is under investigation. At least seven people were injured in the incident, according to Bangkok's Erawan emergency medical centre

items.title: 430,000 UK homeowners face £500-plus jump in monthly mortgage payments
items.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
items.content:

More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

items.title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’
items.author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
items.content:
Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

items.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
items.author: Frédéric Noy
items.content:
It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy

Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.

Finding a room to rent in the UK has become intensely competitive, with prices rising and the number of rooms available shrinking. Have you had to go through lenghty interviews or flatmate “auditions” to secure a space? Thanksgiving is just one day away, but for some Americans, the holiday may look a little different this year as higher costs for food, drinks, household goods, air travel and gasoline have prompted some families to rethink their plans and spending.

Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.
